title: Token Economics, Context Windows & Limits
summary: How token usage turns into cost, latency, and failure modes. Covers the asymmetry between input and output pricing, where unseen tokens come from, the separate limits a request can hit (context window, output cap, rate limits, and spend limits), and how prompt caching and batch processing change the bill. Figures are quoted from provider documentation as read on 2026-09-11 and are expected to change.
objectives: Read a response's usage fields and attribute tokens to uncached input, cached input, output, and thinking, including tokens the user never sees.
Estimate the cost of a workload from published pricing, accounting for the input and output price difference and for tokenizer differences between models.
Distinguish the context window, the output cap, rate limits, and spend limits, and name the signal each one produces.
Evaluate when prompt caching and batch processing reduce cost, and lay out a prompt so that caching can work.

sections.title: Count the tokens you pay for, including the ones you never see
paragraphs: Hosted models meter work in tokens, and the unit is not stable across providers or even across models from one provider. Google's documentation gives a rule of thumb for Gemini: a token is "about 4 characters," and "100 tokens is equal to about 60-80 English words." Anthropic's pricing page notes that Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that "produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text," with the exact increase depending on content. The practical consequence is that a token count measured against one model does not transfer to another. Anthropic's token-counting guide tells developers to "recount prompts against the model you plan to use rather than reusing counts measured against earlier models," and describes its counting endpoint as free to use but an estimate that can differ from actual usage "by a small amount."

A request's bill also includes tokens nobody typed or read. Anthropic's context-window guide lists what counts: the system prompt, every message including tool results, images, and documents, the tool definitions, and the output generated for the turn, "including its extended thinking." Thinking tokens "are billed as output tokens," and Google documents the same for Gemini, where pricing "is based on the full thought tokens the model needs to generate, despite only the summary being output from the API." The reliable instrument is the usage record that each response returns. Anthropic splits input into input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens; Gemini reports input, output, thinking, cached, and tool-use tokens separately. Log these for every request: they are the ground truth that estimates should be reconciled against.

code.label: Reading Anthropic's usage fields (the worked example from its prompt-caching guide)
code.code:
cache_read_input_tokens       100,000   prefix read from the cache
cache_creation_input_tokens         0   nothing new written to the cache
input_tokens                       50   the user message after the cache breakpoint
-------------------------------------------------
total input tokens processed  100,050

total_input_tokens = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens

sections.title: Output costs more than input, and that shapes design
paragraphs: Price lists separate input from output, and output is the expensive side. In Anthropic's pricing table as read on 2026-09-11, every listed model's output rate is five times its input rate: for example, $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens for Claude Opus 5, and $1 and $5 for Claude Haiku 4.5. A workload that reads a long document and returns a short classification is dominated by input cost. One that generates long reports, or thinks at length before answering, is dominated by output cost, and because thinking tokens are billed as output, raising reasoning depth moves spend onto the expensive side of the ledger.

That gives a simple estimating habit: compute input tokens multiplied by the input rate and output tokens multiplied by the output rate separately, count thinking as output, and split the input side into cached and uncached parts when caching is on. Estimate with the tokenizer of the model you will actually use, then reconcile against logged usage after a pilot. Watch for modifiers that sit on top of base rates. Anthropic documents a 1.1x multiplier for US-only inference on Claude 4.6 and later models, and states that on its 1M-token-context models "a 900k-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9k-token request," so there a long context raises the bill in proportion to its length rather than through a surcharge. Treat every figure in this module as dated: prices change, and this module is reviewed on a 30-day cadence for that reason.
sections.callout: Estimate input and output separately. In the pricing read for this module, an output token costs five times an input token.

code.label: Worked estimate for a hypothetical workload at Anthropic's published Claude Haiku 4.5 rates (read 2026-09-11)
code.code:
Rates: input $1.00 per million tokens, output $5.00 per million tokens

10,000 requests x 3,000 input tokens  = 30,000,000 input tokens   ->  $30.00
10,000 requests x   400 output tokens =  4,000,000 output tokens  ->  $20.00
                                                          Total      $50.00

Same workload, 2,000 output tokens per request (for example, long reasoning):
10,000 requests x 2,000 output tokens = 20,000,000 output tokens  -> $100.00
                                                          Total     $130.00

sections.title: Four different limits, four different signals
paragraphs: A request can be refused or cut short at several independent limits, and each produces a different signal. The context window is everything the model can reference "including the response itself." Anthropic lists a 1M-token window for models such as Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5, each able to generate up to 128k output tokens per request, and a 200k-token window for others such as Claude Sonnet 4.5. If the input alone exceeds the window, the API returns a 400 error ("prompt is too long"). If generation reaches the max_tokens you set, the response ends with stop_reason "max_tokens": a successful response that is nonetheless truncated. On Claude 4.5 and newer models, a response that fills the context window ends with "model_context_window_exceeded," which the documentation says to treat as truncated. Google documents a trap specific to thinking models: max_output_tokens includes thought tokens, so a low cap can leave truncated or empty output while the thinking is still billed.

Throughput and spend limits are separate again. Anthropic measures requests per minute, input tokens per minute, and output tokens per minute for each model class; exceeding any of them returns HTTP 429 with a retry-after header. It uses a token-bucket algorithm, so capacity replenishes continuously and short bursts can trip a limit even when the per-minute average looks safe. Spend limits behave differently: when an organization reaches its tier's monthly cap, requests also return 429 but with no retry-after header, and retrying, including SDK automatic retries, "fails until access resumes." An application that treats every 429 as "wait and retry" will spin uselessly against a spend cap. Finally, a larger window is not a free upgrade. Anthropic notes that "as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot," and that cached content still occupies the window: caching "changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count."
sections.callout: Check stop_reason on every response. A successful response with stop_reason "max_tokens" is a truncated answer, not a complete one.

code.label: Route each limit by its own signal (Anthropic Messages API values)
code.code:
if response.stop_reason in ("max_tokens", "model_context_window_exceeded"):
    mark_truncated(response)       # never pass a cut-off answer downstream as complete
elif response.stop_reason == "end_turn":
    accept(response)

# On an HTTP 429 error:
#   retry-after header present -> rate limit: wait that long, then retry with backoff
#   no retry-after header      -> possibly the monthly spend cap: stop retrying and alert a person

sections.title: Caching and batching change the bill, if the prompt is built for them
paragraphs: Prompt caching reuses the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix, and the economics look similar across providers. Anthropic prices a 5-minute cache write at 1.25x the base input price, a 1-hour write at 2x, and a cache read at 0.1x, so caching "pays off after one cache read for the 5-minute duration (1.25x write), or after two cache reads for the 1-hour duration (2x write)." OpenAI describes cached input as "discounted up to 90%"; for GPT-5.6 and later it prices writes at 1.25x and reads at 0.1x the uncached input rate, keeps a prefix eligible for reuse for 30 minutes after its last write or reuse, and requires at least 1,024 tokens before a prefix can be cached. Anthropic also documents that for most Claude models cache reads do not count toward the input-tokens-per-minute rate limit, so caching raises effective throughput as well as lowering cost.

Caching only works if the prompt is laid out for it. Both providers match on the prefix. Anthropic caches "the entire prompt - tools, system, and messages (in that order)" up to a cache breakpoint, and changing any block at or before the breakpoint produces a different hash on the next request. OpenAI advises putting "stable developer instructions and shared reference material first" and moving timestamps and user-specific content to the end. A timestamp on the first line of a system prompt defeats caching on every request. Prompts shorter than the model's minimum are processed without caching "and no error is returned," so confirm caching in the usage fields rather than assuming it. For work that does not need an immediate answer, batch processing is the other lever: Anthropic documents a 50% discount on both input and output tokens for its Batch API, and OpenAI documents a 50% discount, a 24-hour completion window, and a separate pool of rate limits for its batches. Anthropic states that batch and caching discounts can be combined.
sections.callout: Stable content first, variable content last. The layout that lets caching work also keeps prompts easier to audit.

activity.title: Build a token budget and limit plan for one workflow
instructions: Step 1: Choose one workflow you run or plan to run through an AI API or tool, such as summarizing incoming support tickets, and write down its expected daily request volume.

Step 2: Take three representative inputs and count their tokens with the provider's counting tool for the exact model you will use, or run them once and read the usage fields in the responses. Record uncached input, cached input, output, and thinking tokens separately.
Step 3: Using the provider's current published rates, and recording the date you read them, compute the daily cost of the workflow with input and output priced separately.

Step 4: Mark which parts of the prompt are identical on every request and which vary. Reorder the prompt so the stable part comes first, and state whether that stable part meets the model's minimum cacheable length.
Step 5: For each of the four limits (context window, output cap, rate limit, spend limit), write the signal your application would receive and the action it should take.
evidence: A token table for three representative inputs showing uncached input, cached input, output, and thinking tokens, with the counting method named.
A daily cost estimate showing the formula, the rates used, and the date those rates were read.
A four-row limit table listing each limit, its signal (HTTP status, header, or stop_reason), and the action your application takes.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which single change (shorter outputs, less reasoning depth, caching, or batching) would move your estimate most, and what would it cost you in quality or latency?

questions.prompt: A response arrives successfully with stop_reason "max_tokens". What should the application conclude?
choices: The answer is complete and safe to use
The answer was cut off at the output cap: raise max_tokens or continue the response, and do not treat it as complete
The request was rate limited and should be retried after the retry-after interval
The input exceeded the context window
questions.explanation: stop_reason "max_tokens" means generation reached the limit you set, so the response is truncated even though the request succeeded. Rate limiting returns an HTTP 429 error, and input that exceeds the context window returns a 400 error; neither produces a successful response.

questions.prompt: An application receives HTTP 429 from Anthropic's API with no retry-after header. What is a likely cause, and what should the application avoid?
choices: A short burst exceeded requests per minute, so it should retry immediately in a tight loop
The prompt was longer than the context window
The organization may have reached its monthly spend cap; retries will keep failing until access resumes, so stop retrying and alert a person
The response reached max_tokens
questions.explanation: Anthropic documents that rate-limit 429s carry a retry-after header, while the 429 returned at a spend cap does not, and retries fail until access resumes. Tight retry loops never help. Context-window and max_tokens conditions produce a 400 error and a stop_reason respectively, not a 429.

questions.prompt: At $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, which costs more: 1,000,000 input tokens with 100,000 output tokens, or 200,000 input tokens with 400,000 output tokens?
choices: The first, because it uses more tokens in total
They cost the same
They cannot be compared without knowing the context window size
The second: $2.20 against $1.50, because output tokens cost five times as much
questions.explanation: First workload: $1.00 input plus $0.50 output is $1.50. Second: $0.20 input plus $2.00 output is $2.20. Total token count is misleading when input and output are priced differently, and the context window size does not affect the per-token price in this comparison.

questions.prompt: A team adds the current timestamp as the first line of a long, otherwise unchanging system prompt. What happens to prompt caching?
choices: The prefix changes on every request, so there are no cache reads; stable content should come first and dynamic content last
Nothing, because caching ignores timestamps
Caching improves because every request is now unique
The API rejects the request with an error
questions.explanation: Caching matches on the prompt prefix, and changing any block at or before a cache breakpoint produces a different hash. OpenAI and Anthropic both advise placing dynamic content such as timestamps at the end. The API does not error; it simply processes the prompt without a cache hit.

questions.prompt: Why should a token count measured on one model not be reused to budget for another model?
choices: Token counts depend only on word count, so they are always identical
Tokenizers differ between models: Anthropic documents its newer tokenizer producing roughly 30% more tokens for the same text
Only output tokens are counted, so input counts do not matter
All providers share one tokenizer, so the counts are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Tokenization is model-specific, which is why Anthropic tells developers to recount prompts against the model they plan to use. Token counts are not word counts, input tokens are billed, and providers do not share a tokenizer.

questions.prompt: Which statement about thinking tokens is supported by both Anthropic and Google documentation?
choices: They are free, because usually only a summary is shown
They count toward the context window but never toward cost
They are billed at the cached-input rate
They are billed as output, including thinking that is not shown in full
questions.explanation: Anthropic states that thinking tokens are billed as output tokens; Google states that pricing is based on the full thought tokens generated even though only a summary is returned. They are neither free nor billed at the cached-input rate.
